    "situatedness": {
      "dimension_name": "Situatedness",
      "dimension_description": "How the story positions itself in literary space: genre affiliation and fidelity, metafictional self-awareness, intertextuality, structural ambition, thematic self-consciousness, and its assumed reader.",
      "aspects": {
        "genre_positioning": {
          "aspect_name": "Genre Affiliation, Fidelity, and Tone",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "SIT_GEN_001",
              "name": "Primary Genre Category",
              "question": "What is the story's primary genre classification based on its dominant setting, plot devices, and reader expectations?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "realist_contemporary",
                "historical_realist",
                "science_fiction",
                "fantasy",
                "horror",
                "mystery_detective",
                "thriller_suspense",
                "romance",
                "comedy_satire",
                "myth_fable_fairy_tale",
                "literary_realist_fiction",
                "multi_genre_blend",
                "nonfictional_mode_pastiche_or_essayistic"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Identify the dominant setting (realistic vs speculative), core plot engine (investigation, romance, quest, etc.), and conventional markers (magic, technology, monsters, clues) to assign the genre that best matches the story's main reader contract."
            },
            {
              "id": "SIT_GEN_002",
              "name": "Genre Fidelity Mode",
              "question": "How does the story relate to the conventions of its primary genre?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "straight_genre_fulfillment",
                "crossgenre_blend",
                "genre_subversion_inversion",
                "genre_frame_with_different_primary_focus",
                "genre_agnostic_experimental"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Compare the story's structure, tropes, and resolution to standard examples in the primary genre: does it mostly follow them, combine with another genre, deliberately invert expectations (e.g. refusing a mystery solution), use genre only as a loose frame for other aims, or resist stable genre classification?"
            },
            {
              "id": "SIT_GEN_003",
              "name": "Genre Signal Timing",
              "question": "How early in the story does the text clearly signal its primary genre to the reader?",
              "type": "ordinal",
              "values": [
                "immediate (within opening paragraph)",
                "early (within the first scene/page)",
                "mid-story (after some neutral buildup)",
                "late/ambiguous (genre only clear near the end or never fully fixed)"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Locate the first decisive cue to genre (e.g., explicit magic, a corpse and cop, spaceship, meet-cute). Judge its position relative to total length and whether earlier passages are generically neutral."
            },
            {
              "id": "SIT_GEN_004",
              "name": "Tone Toward Genre Conventions",
              "question": "What is the dominant tonal stance the story takes toward its own genre conventions?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "earnest_sincere",
                "lightly_ironic_playful",
                "parodic_or_spoofing",
                "critical_or_deconstructive",
                "nostalgic_reverent",
                "ambivalently_mixed"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Assess narration and dialogue for signals of mockery, affectionate exaggeration, or critique of genre tropes; determine whether the text mainly treats its genre devices straight, gently jokes about them, outright spoofs them, uses them to critique the genre, or combines these attitudes."
            },
            {
              "id": "SIT_GEN_005",
              "name": "Narrated Genre Awareness",
              "question": "To what degree does the narration show explicit awareness of operating within a genre (e.g. by naming tropes or commenting on them)?",
              "type": "ordinal",
              "values": [
                "no_explicit_genre_awareness",
                "implicit_winks_or_subtle_signals",
                "overt_commentary_on_genre_tropes"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Look for lines where the narrator mentions things like 'as in all good horror stories' or 'this wasn't how romances are supposed to go'; subtle irony without explicit naming counts as 'implicit_winks', while direct references to genre patterns count as 'overt_commentary'."
            }
          ]
        },
        "genre_orientation": {
          "aspect_name": "Genre Orientation and Use",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "SIT_GEN_006",
              "name": "Plot vs Atmosphere Orientation",
              "question": "Is the story's use of genre more driven by plot mechanics or by mood and atmosphere?",
              "type": "ordinal",
              "values": [
                "1-Strongly plot-driven",
                "2-Mixed but leaning plot",
                "3-Balanced",
                "4-Mixed but leaning atmosphere",
                "5-Strongly atmosphere-driven"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Assess whether narrative energy is mainly invested in advancing external events and twists (plot) or in sustaining tone, mood, and setting texture (atmosphere). Use proportion of text devoted to action vs description and interiority as cues."
            },
            {
              "id": "SIT_GEN_009",
              "name": "Assumed Reader Competence",
              "question": "What level of genre or literary competence does the story assume of its reader?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "General reader (no specialized knowledge assumed)",
                "Genre-savvy reader (expects familiarity with specific genre tropes)",
                "Literary-educated reader (expects comfort with complex structures/allusions)",
                "Insider/series reader (expects prior knowledge of specific fictional universe)"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Look for unexplained references to prior works, in-universe jargon, complex structural games, or meta-genre talk. Infer the implied audience from how much the story relies on pre-existing genre literacy or series knowledge.",
              "merged_from": [
                "SIT_MET_014",
                "SIT_MET_401"
              ]
            },
            {
              "id": "SIT_GEN_010",
              "name": "Moral / Philosophical Weighting",
              "question": "Relative to entertainment, how important are moral or philosophical arguments in the story's overall design?",
              "type": "scale",
              "values": [
                "1",
                "2",
                "3",
                "4",
                "5"
              ],
              "detection_method": "On a 1\u20135 scale, judge how far the text foregrounds explicit ethical debates, thematic exposition, or philosophical reflection versus prioritizing suspense, adventure, or sensory pleasure. Consider narrator commentary and climactic speeches."
            }
          ]
        },
        "metafictional_self_awareness": {
          "aspect_name": "Metafiction and Narrative Self-Awareness",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "SIT_MET_004",
              "name": "Fourth-Wall Permeability",
              "question": "To what extent does the story break or blur the boundary between story-world and reader?",
              "type": "ordinal",
              "values": [
                "1-No fourth-wall breaking (reader never acknowledged)",
                "2-Implicit winks or aside-like tonal gestures",
                "3-Occasional direct address or acknowledgement of reader",
                "4-Consistent or radical fourth-wall violations"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Note any direct reader address, instructions, or acknowledgements. Also consider subtler asides that presume the reader's complicity. Judge overall pattern to place on the 1\u20134 scale."
            },
            {
              "id": "SIT_MET_006",
              "name": "Embedded Storytelling Scenes",
              "question": "Does the story include significant in-world acts of storytelling (characters telling stories, reading letters, viewing media) that shape its meaning?",
              "type": "ordinal",
              "values": [
                "0-None",
                "1-Minor (brief anecdote or reference)",
                "2-Moderate (one substantial embedded story or document)",
                "3-Extensive (multiple or structurally central embedded narratives/documents)"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Count occasions where characters narrate past events, read/view stories, or consult documents that themselves have narrative form. Rate intensity based on their length and structural importance to plot or theme."
            }
          ]
        },
        "metafiction_selfreflexivity": {
          "aspect_name": "Metafiction & Narrative Self-Reflexivity",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "SIT_MET_002",
              "name": "Fourth-Wall Breaking",
              "question": "Does the narration or a character directly address the reader or audience as such?",
              "type": "binary",
              "values": [
                "no direct address",
                "yes, direct address present"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Look for second-person plural or singular addresses like 'you, dear reader', 'let me tell you', or direct comments assuming an audience outside the story-world. Ignore in-world second-person dialogue between characters."
            },
            {
              "id": "SIT_MET_005",
              "name": "Ontological Play & Reality Instability",
              "question": "How does the story treat the stability of its fictional reality (e.g., dreams, simulations, nested fictions)?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "stable mimetic reality (no questioning of what is real)",
                "single speculative layer but ontologically stable (e.g., one magical or SF premise taken as given)",
                "ambiguous/unstable reality (reader encouraged to doubt whether events are real, dreamt, simulated, etc.)",
                "multiple explicit reality layers or nested fictions (stories, simulations, or games within the world, with movement between levels)"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Note whether characters or narrator question reality, and whether the text establishes dream/sim boundaries or multiple diegetic levels. Classify based on the strongest ontological device governing interpretation."
            }
          ]
        },
        "intertextuality_tradition": {
          "aspect_name": "Intertextuality & Relation to Tradition",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "SIT_MET_009",
              "name": "Attitude Toward Literary Tradition",
              "question": "How does the story position itself emotionally and critically toward the literary or mythic traditions it engages?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "reverent/continuist (aims mainly to honour, preserve, or smoothly extend tradition)",
                "critical/revisionist (explicitly reinterprets or challenges inherited stories)",
                "parodic/irreverent (treats tradition primarily as material for jokes or send-up)",
                "eclectic/agnostic (borrows elements without clear evaluative stance toward the sources)"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Consider tone around inherited plots/figures: is there nostalgia, anger, subversion, mockery, or neutral remixing? Choose the category that best captures the dominant stance."
            },
            {
              "id": "SIT_MET_202",
              "name": "Intertextual Strategy Types",
              "question": "What kinds of intertextual engagement with other works or traditions does the story employ?",
              "type": "multi_select",
              "values": [
                "explicit_named_reference_to_specific_texts_or_authors",
                "retelling_or_reframing_of_specific_canonical_story",
                "stylistic_pastiche_of_identifiable_author_or_period",
                "use_of_mythological_or_religious_source_material",
                "self_referential_links_to_other_works_in_same_storyworld"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Identify whether the text (a) names specific books, authors, films, etc.; (b) clearly retells or inverts a known story; (c) imitates a recognizable style (e.g. Doyle pastiche); (d) draws on myth/religion beyond generic reference; or (e) references prior stories in the same sequence; select all that apply."
            }
          ]
        },
        "intertextual_positioning": {
          "aspect_name": "Intertextuality and Relation to Tradition",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "SIT_MET_008",
              "name": "Reference Explicitness",
              "question": "Are intertextual gestures primarily explicit name-checks or more diffuse, generic echoes?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "None (no discernible references)",
                "Primarily explicit named references (titles, authors, specific works)",
                "Primarily implicit echoes (genres, archetypes, unnamed myths)",
                "Balanced mix of explicit and implicit"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Distinguish between overt citations (e.g., naming Shakespeare, Star Wars) and subtler patterning where the story mirrors recognizable myths or genres without naming them. Classify based on the dominant mode."
            }
          ]
        },
        "literary_register_structure": {
          "aspect_name": "Literary Register & Structural Ambition",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "SIT_MET_012",
              "name": "Literary Ambition Signaling",
              "question": "What kind of literary ambition does the story appear to signal in terms of market positioning and aesthetic aim?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "primarily genre entertainment (plot- and trope-driven, minimal overt thematic or stylistic ambition)",
                "crossover genre with literary aspirations (genre frame but clear stylistic/thematic ambition)",
                "mainstream literary fiction (character and theme foregrounded over genre engines)",
                "formally experimental/avant-garde (structure or language foregrounded over conventional readability)"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Integrate cues from prose density, structural play, thematic explicitness, and reliance on genre scaffolds to infer whether the piece reads like commercial genre fiction, a hybrid, mainstream 'lit fic', or deliberate formal experiment."
            }
          ]
        },
        "metafiction_self_consciousness": {
          "aspect_name": "Metafiction and Narrative Self-Consciousness",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "SIT_MET_102",
              "name": "Ending-Level Self-Commentary on Story",
              "question": "Does the ending explicitly comment on the act of storytelling, narrative closure, or the status of this text as a story?",
              "type": "binary",
              "values": [
                "no",
                "yes"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Inspect the final page or paragraph for statements that generalize about endings ('stories don't really end'), refer to the narrative just told ('and that is how I came to write this'), or otherwise step back from the diegesis; mark 'yes' if such commentary is present."
            },
            {
              "id": "SIT_MET_103",
              "name": "Embedded Narrative Structures",
              "question": "Does the story incorporate stories-within-the-story, such as framed tales, letters, reports, or other internal texts that characters tell or read?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "none",
                "single_embedded_narrative_or_document",
                "multiple_embedded_narratives_or_documents"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Identify whether there is a distinct internal narrative unit (e.g. a long letter, a character's told anecdote, a dossier) separated structurally or typographically from the main narration; if more than one such internal text or tale appears, select 'multiple'."
            },
            {
              "id": "SIT_MET_104",
              "name": "Narrator Address Mode",
              "question": "How, if at all, does the narrator address a 'you' in the text?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "no_direct_address",
                "generic_second_person_as_generalization",
                "direct_address_to_actual_reader",
                "address_to_diegetic_listener_only"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Locate any second-person pronouns in the narration; judge whether 'you' is used generically ('you never know when...'), clearly aimed at the real reader ('dear reader', 'you reading this'), or directed to an in-world listener (e.g. a confidant or interrogator being spoken to)."
            }
          ]
        },
        "literary_positioning_structure": {
          "aspect_name": "Literary Ambition, Style, and Structural Experimentation",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "SIT_MET_301",
              "name": "Perceived Literary Ambition in Prose Style",
              "question": "How marked and 'literary' is the prose style in terms of figurative language, rhythm, and syntactic complexity?",
              "type": "scale",
              "values": [
                1,
                2,
                3,
                4,
                5
              ],
              "detection_method": "Rate 1 if sentences are short, plain, and utilitarian with minimal figurative language; 3 if there is a noticeable but moderate use of metaphor and rhythmic variation; 5 if the prose is dense with imagery, unusual syntax, and stylistic foregrounding that demands interpretive attention.",
              "merged_from": [
                "SIT_MET_010"
              ]
            },
            {
              "id": "SIT_MET_302",
              "name": "Structural Experimentation Level",
              "question": "How conventional or experimental is the story's overall structural arrangement (timelines, sections, points of view)?",
              "type": "ordinal",
              "values": [
                "simple_linear_single_strand",
                "framed_or_mildly_non_linear",
                "strongly_fragmented_or_formally_experimental"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Map the sequence of events and narrative frames: if events proceed in straightforward chronological order with one main narrator, choose 'simple_linear'; if there is a frame story, a few flashbacks, or one notable time-jump, choose 'framed_or_mildly_non_linear'; if the text uses fragments, multiple time loops, unusual sectioning, or mixed media, choose 'strongly_fragmented_or_formally_experimental'.",
              "merged_from": [
                "SIT_GEN_008"
              ]
            },
            {
              "id": "SIT_MET_303",
              "name": "Thematic Explicitness and Moralizing",
              "question": "How explicitly does the story articulate its themes or morals in the narration or character speech?",
              "type": "scale",
              "values": [
                1,
                2,
                3,
                4,
                5
              ],
              "detection_method": "Rate 1 when themes remain implicit and never spelled out; 3 when characters or narrator occasionally state generalizations about life or the story's issues; 5 when the story includes clear thesis-like statements or overt morals summarizing how readers should interpret events.",
              "merged_from": [
                "PLT_THM_002",
                "STY_TON_022",
                "SIT_MET_011",
                "SIT_MET_013"
              ]
            }
          ]
        },
        "reader_positioning": {
          "aspect_name": "Assumed Reader Knowledge and In-Group Positioning",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "SIT_MET_402",
              "name": "Required External Knowledge Level",
              "question": "How much non-everyday external knowledge (historical, theoretical, niche cultural) is required to fully understand the story's stakes or references?",
              "type": "ordinal",
              "values": [
                "none_beyond_everyday_life",
                "some_background_helpful_but_not_essential",
                "substantial_background_required_for_full_comprehension"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Note references to specific historical events, theories, subcultures, or technical matters: if comprehension is possible without them, choose 'none' or 'some_background_helpful'; if key plot or thematic points are opaque without such knowledge, choose 'substantial_background_required'."
            },
            {
              "id": "SIT_MET_403",
              "name": "Jargon and In-Group Reference Density",
              "question": "How densely does the story use specialized jargon, acronyms, or insider cultural references without explanation?",
              "type": "ordinal",
              "values": [
                "none_or_minimal",
                "moderate_and_mostly_explained",
                "dense_and_largely_unexplained"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Scan for technical terms, abbreviations, or niche slang: if rare or always glossed in context, select 'none_or_minimal' or 'moderate_and_mostly_explained'; if such language is frequent and often left unexplained, select 'dense_and_largely_unexplained'."
            }
          ]
        },
        "thematic_self_awareness": {
          "aspect_name": "Thematic Self-Awareness and Moral Stance",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "SIT_MET_501",
              "name": "Narratorial Thematic Commentary Presence",
              "question": "Does the narrator explicitly comment on the story's themes, lessons, or the meaning of events beyond characters' situated perspectives?",
              "type": "binary",
              "values": [
                "no",
                "yes"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Identify passages where the narrating voice (not just a character) generalizes about what the events show (e.g. 'That is how people are', 'It was then she learned that...'); if such commentary appears, mark 'yes'."
            }
          ]
        }
      }
    },
    "temporal_structure": {
      "dimension_name": "Temporal Structure",
      "dimension_description": "Time handling: duration, order, pacing, frequency, temporal manipulation",
      "aspects": {
        "span_and_pacing": {
          "aspect_name": "Temporal Span and Pacing",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "TMP_DUR_002",
              "name": "Narrative Time Compression",
              "question": "How compressed is the narrative relative to its story-time span (how much calendar time is covered per page on average)?",
              "type": "scale",
              "values": [
                1,
                2,
                3,
                4,
                5
              ],
              "detection_method": "Estimate the amount of story-time typically covered in a page or paragraph. Rate 1 if the narrative largely unfolds in real time with minimal summary; 5 if it routinely leaps across weeks, years, or generations in a few lines, with intermediate values for mixed or moderate compression."
            }
          ]
        },
        "pacing_and_frequency": {
          "aspect_name": "Pacing, Scene/Summary, and Frequency",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "TMP_DUR_004",
              "name": "Dominant pacing mode",
              "question": "Which pacing mode dominates the narrative?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "scene_dominant",
                "mixed_no_clear_dominant",
                "summary_dominant",
                "montage_or_episode_chain"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Identify whether the text primarily consists of extended scene units, extended summarizing narration, or a chain of short set-pieces separated by explicit jumps. Classify as montage/episode_chain if the story moves through many relatively brief, self-contained episodes that each reset time/place."
            }
          ]
        },
        "anchoring_and_pressure": {
          "aspect_name": "Temporal Anchoring and Time Pressure",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "TMP_DUR_006",
              "name": "Use of Iterative or Habitual Narration",
              "question": "Does the narrative explicitly use iterative or habitual constructions (e.g., 'every Sunday we would...', 'for years she always...') to summarize repeated events?",
              "type": "binary",
              "values": [
                "yes",
                "no"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Look for passages that condense recurring behavior into generalized time (using adverbs like 'always', 'often', 'every day') rather than specifying single occasions."
            },
            {
              "id": "TMP_DUR_009",
              "name": "Density of Explicit Time Markers",
              "question": "How frequently does the narrative use explicit temporal markers or transitions such as 'later that night', 'the next morning', 'weeks passed'?",
              "type": "scale",
              "values": [
                1,
                2,
                3,
                4,
                5
              ],
              "detection_method": "Count or estimate occurrences of overt time-advancing phrases. Rate 1 if such markers are rare and time shifts are mostly implicit; 5 if almost every scene change is accompanied by an explicit temporal phrase.",
              "merged_from": [
                "TMP_ORD_013",
                "TMP_ORD_022"
              ]
            },
            {
              "id": "TMP_DUR_010",
              "name": "Typical Inter-Scene Time Jump Magnitude",
              "question": "What is the typical magnitude of time that elapses between consecutive scenes or sections?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "continuous_or_near_continuous (minutes)",
                "hours_to_single_day",
                "multi_day_to_few_weeks",
                "months_or_longer_between_scenes"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Examine transitions between scenes or numbered/white-space-separated sections and infer the approximate time skipped; choose the category that best represents the common pattern."
            }
          ]
        },
        "pacing_and_summary": {
          "aspect_name": "Pacing, Scene vs Summary, and Ellipsis",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "TMP_DUR_007",
              "name": "Ellipsis frequency category",
              "question": "How frequently does the narrative leap over substantial stretches of story time via ellipsis (e.g., 'weeks passed', 'years later') without narrating or closely summarizing intervening action?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "minimal_ellipses",
                "some_ellipses",
                "frequent_large_ellipses"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Count occurrences of explicit large time-jumps and judge what proportion of the story's progress is carried by such leaps; classify as minimal (rare), some (occasional but not dominant), or frequent (core structuring device)."
            }
          ]
        },
        "anchoring_and_segmentation": {
          "aspect_name": "Temporal Anchoring and Segmentation",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "TMP_DUR_008",
              "name": "Precision of temporal anchoring",
              "question": "How precise are the explicit temporal markers (dates, times, seasons) used to locate events in time?",
              "type": "ordinal",
              "values": [
                "1_vague_or_no_markers",
                "2_seasonal_or_general_period_markers",
                "3_relative_day_and_duration_markers",
                "4_exact_calendar_dates_and_clock_times"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Search for explicit time expressions: vague ('long ago', 'that winter'), seasonal ('in spring', 'that summer'), relative but quantified ('three days later', 'for six months'), or precise ('14 March 1952', 'at 3:47 a.m.'). Rate according to the highest level of precision that recurs systematically, not isolated one-off mentions."
            }
          ]
        },
        "perspective_and_tense": {
          "aspect_name": "Temporal Perspective and Tense",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "TMP_DUR_011",
              "name": "Dominant Narrative Tense",
              "question": "In what tense is the bulk of the narrative discourse written?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "past",
                "present",
                "future",
                "mixed_or_shifted"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Identify the grammatical tense used in most narrative sentences (excluding dialogue). If tense shifts markedly between large sections, classify as 'mixed_or_shifted'.",
              "merged_from": [
                "TMP_DUR_015"
              ]
            },
            {
              "id": "TMP_DUR_012",
              "name": "Narrator's Temporal Distance from Events",
              "question": "From what temporal vantage point does the narrator tell the story relative to the events (simultaneous or retrospective)?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "simultaneous_or_ongoing (narration_occurs_as_events_unfold)",
                "slightly_retrospective (days_to_few_years_after)",
                "distant_retrospective (many_years_or_decades_after)",
                "multiple_temporal_vantages_mixed"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Look for cues such as past-tense reflection ('years later I realized'), adult hindsight on childhood events, or explicit dates indicating how far after the events the telling occurs. Classify accordingly, or as mixed if different sections clearly use different vantage points."
            }
          ]
        },
        "chronological_ordering": {
          "aspect_name": "Chronological Ordering and Anachrony",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "TMP_ORD_001",
              "name": "Global Chronological Structure",
              "question": "How closely does the order of presented events follow chronological story-time order?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "strictly_chronological",
                "mostly_chronological_with_rare_flashbacks",
                "chronological_spine_with_frequent_flashbacks",
                "strongly_non_linear_or_fragmented",
                "reverse_chronology_dominant"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Map major events in story time and compare to their presentation order. Categorize based on whether there are only minor deviations, many embedded analepses, heavy fragmentation, or an overall backward ordering."
            },
            {
              "id": "TMP_ORD_004",
              "name": "Depth of Flashback Nesting",
              "question": "How deeply are flashbacks nested inside other temporal layers?",
              "type": "ordinal",
              "values": [
                "no_flashbacks",
                "single_level_flashbacks_only",
                "multi_level_nested_flashbacks"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Examine whether flashbacks occur only from the primary narrative present, or whether there are flashbacks inside flashbacks (e.g., a character in a remembered scene recalling an even earlier event). Classify nesting depth accordingly."
            },
            {
              "id": "TMP_ORD_005",
              "name": "Backstory Placement Strategy",
              "question": "Where in the narrative are key backstory revelations concentrated?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "front_loaded_exposition",
                "evenly_interleaved_throughout",
                "withheld_until_late_reveal",
                "minimal_or_implict_backstory_only"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Identify when the text supplies crucial past events explaining present conflict. Determine whether these are provided mainly at the beginning, woven steadily throughout, reserved for a late twist, or largely omitted/implied.",
              "merged_from": [
                "TMP_ORD_020",
                "AGENT_ATTR_025"
              ]
            },
            {
              "id": "TMP_ORD_010",
              "name": "Degree of Chronological Discontinuity",
              "question": "How often and how sharply does the narrative jump across time in ways that disrupt straightforward chronological flow?",
              "type": "scale",
              "values": [
                1,
                2,
                3,
                4,
                5
              ],
              "detection_method": "Assess the frequency and magnitude of temporal jumps (backwards or forwards) that interrupt linear progression. Rate 1 if the story moves smoothly forward with only small, well-signposted skips; 5 if it frequently leaps or shuffles in time, requiring active reconstruction."
            }
          ]
        },
        "order_and_anachrony": {
          "aspect_name": "Chronological Order and Anachrony",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "TMP_ORD_002",
              "name": "Anachrony intensity",
              "question": "On a 1\u20135 scale, how heavily does the narrative rely on explicit flashbacks or flash-forwards as structural devices?",
              "type": "scale",
              "values": [
                "1_no_real_anachrony",
                "2_rare_or_minor_flashbacks",
                "3_regular_flashbacks_supporting_main_line",
                "4_frequent_or_extended_anachrony",
                "5_dominant_anachronic_structure"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Count and evaluate the size of departures from the current present (multi-line or scene-level analepses/prolepses rather than quick references). Rate 1 if absent; 2 if there are only one or two brief backstory scenes; 3 if intermittent flashbacks are used but the main spine is forward; 4 if shifts are frequent or long; 5 if the story's logic depends on a heavily rearranged order (e.g., epistolary variations, nested timelines)."
            },
            {
              "id": "TMP_ORD_007",
              "name": "Number of interwoven temporal strands",
              "question": "How many distinct temporal strands (e.g., periods or lifelines) are interwoven in the discourse, as opposed to appearing only in isolated flashback blocks?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "single_strand",
                "two_main_strands_braided",
                "three_or_more_strands_braided"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Identify recurring alternations among different time levels (e.g., present vs childhood vs ancestor centuries) that return multiple times and are cross-cut rather than told in one chunk. Count how many such strands are substantially sustained and choose category accordingly.",
              "merged_from": [
                "TMP_ORD_016"
              ]
            }
          ]
        },
        "chronological_order_and_anachrony": {
          "aspect_name": "Chronological Order, Frames, and Anachrony",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "TMP_ORD_012",
              "name": "Explicit time loops or multi-version retellings",
              "question": "Does the story explicitly present multiple distinct versions or iterations of essentially the same time interval (e.g., execution morning, restaurant lunch), treated as alternates or loops rather than simple memories?",
              "type": "binary",
              "values": [
                "yes",
                "no"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Identify whether the narrative clearly resets the clock to the same starting moment and then narrates divergent sequences (as in Rashomon-style or groundhog-day-like structures). Ignore ordinary flashbacks that merely recall a past event once.",
              "merged_from": [
                "TMP_ORD_006"
              ]
            },
            {
              "id": "TMP_ORD_014",
              "name": "Ending temporal scope",
              "question": "Relative to the main line of events, where in story time does the narrative end?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "ends_at_or_just_after_main_climax_no_forward_jump",
                "ends_with_brief_forward_epilogue_or_flashforward",
                "ends_before_external_resolution_mid_arc_or_cliffhanger",
                "ends_at_distant_future_or_far_past_vantage_summarizing_long_term"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Identify the last narrated scene and determine whether it coincides with the primary external resolution, follows it by a short look ahead, stops earlier while major external consequences are offstage, or jumps far ahead (or back) to survey long-term outcomes from another era."
            }
          ]
        },
        "temporal_devices_and_perspective": {
          "aspect_name": "Temporal Devices, Perspective, and Transitions",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "TMP_ORD_011",
              "name": "Dreams/visions as temporal distortion",
              "question": "Does the narrative include extended dream or vision sequences that noticeably distort or suspend ordinary time (e.g., timeless realms, deep-time glimpses, compressed life reviews)?",
              "type": "binary",
              "values": [
                "no_significant_dream_time",
                "significant_dream_or_vision_time"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Identify segments explicitly framed as dreams, visions, or hallucinatory journeys that alter normal temporal experience (e.g., traveling through aeons, talking with dead in timeless spaces) and occupy more than a brief paragraph.",
              "merged_from": [
                "TMP_DUR_017"
              ]
            }
          ]
        },
        "frames_loops_and_frequency": {
          "aspect_name": "Frames, Loops, and Narrative Frequency",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "TMP_ORD_008",
              "name": "Temporal Loop or Reset Pattern",
              "question": "Does the narrative explicitly reset time to an earlier point (looping the same period), and how is this structured?",
              "type": "multi_select",
              "values": [
                "no_explicit_temporal_loop",
                "same_day_or_hour_resets (Groundhog_Day_style)",
                "simulation_or_experiment_resets",
                "branching_restarts_from_key_decision_point",
                "structure_as_infinite_or_unresolved_loop"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Identify mechanisms where the narrative returns to an earlier temporal point while acknowledging prior runs (e.g., characters remembering or records accumulating). Categorize the loop type(s) according to how the reset is motivated and presented."
            },
            {
              "id": "TMP_ORD_009",
              "name": "Dominant Narrative Frequency Mode",
              "question": "Which narrative frequency mode is dominant in presenting main events (how often events are narrated vs occur)?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "singulative (events_told_once_as_they_occur)",
                "iterative (repeated_events_summarized_as_one)",
                "repeating (same_event_retold_multiple_times)",
                "mixed_without_single_dominant_mode"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Assess whether the text primarily narrates each event once in the order it happens, compresses repeated behaviors into iterative summaries, repeatedly revisits the same event from new angles, or uses a balanced mix without a clear predominance."
            }
          ]
        },
        "global_span_and_scope": {
          "aspect_name": "Global Temporal Span and Biographical Scope",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "TMP_DUR_021",
              "name": "Character aging and biographical scope",
              "question": "How much of the focal character(s)' life-course does the story explicitly cover?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "no_significant_aging_single_life_phase",
                "single_character_across_multiple_life_stages",
                "multi_generational_or_system_level_history"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Track whether the same focal character is shown at only one stable age, at clearly different ages/stages (e.g., child and adult), or whether the narrative instead moves across generations or largely treats characters as instances in a long institutional/history arc."
            }
          ]
        },
        "temporal_markers_and_transitions": {
          "aspect_name": "Temporal Markers, Anchoring, and Transitions",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "TMP_DUR_018",
              "name": "Use of seasons and cyclical time as structuring devices",
              "question": "To what extent does the story use seasons, festivals, or other cyclical temporal markers to structure its progression?",
              "type": "scale",
              "values": [
                "1_no_or_negligible_reference_to_seasons_or_cycles",
                "2_occasional_season_or_holiday_mentions_not_structural",
                "3_seasons_or_cycles_mark_a_few_key_turning_points",
                "4_story_progression_is_strongly_keyed_to_seasons_or_festivals",
                "5_seasonal_or_cyclical_markers_form_the_primary_structural_scaffold"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Look for references to seasons (winter, spring), annual holidays, or ritual cycles; judge whether they simply color the setting or actively demarcate narrative phases or provide the main temporal rhythm."
            },
            {
              "id": "TMP_DUR_019",
              "name": "Prevalence of time-of-day markers",
              "question": "How prominently and frequently does the narrative mark times of day (dawn, noon, dusk, midnight, specific hours) to pace scenes?",
              "type": "ordinal",
              "values": [
                "1_almost_no_time_of_day_markers",
                "2_rare_mentions_of_general_times_of_day",
                "3_regular_but_not_systematic_time_of_day_marking",
                "4_frequent_and_specific_time_of_day_references",
                "5_time_of_day_markers_used_as_key_pacing_and_structural_cues"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Count references to times of day; consider both general labels (dawn, evening) and precise clock times; classify based on how systematically these are used to pace or organize scenes."
            }
          ]
        },
        "time_pressure_and_deadlines": {
          "aspect_name": "Time Pressure, Countdown, and Urgency",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "TMP_DUR_013",
              "name": "Presence of explicit ticking clock or deadline",
              "question": "Is there an explicit temporal deadline, countdown, or time-limited window that creates pressure on characters' actions (e.g., execution at 6 a.m., siege before dawn, exam at 9:00)?",
              "type": "binary",
              "values": [
                "yes",
                "no"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Look for clearly defined time limits mentioned as constraints on decisions or actions (fixed hours, days, or countdowns), and whether narrative tension is organized around beating or failing that clock.",
              "merged_from": [
                "REV_SUS_006",
                "TMP_ORD_015"
              ]
            }
          ]
        }
      }
    },
    "agents": {
      "dimension_name": "Agents",
      "dimension_description": "Characters: identities, roles, attributes, emotions, motivations, archetypes",
      "aspects": {
        "character_inventory_identity": {
          "aspect_name": "Character Inventory & Identity",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ID_001",
              "name": "Scope of named human agents",
              "question": "How many distinct named human characters (with proper names) appear in the narrative, excluding purely collective labels like 'the villagers'?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "1",
                "2-3",
                "4-6",
                "7+"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Scan the text for human characters referred to by proper names (e.g., 'Maria', 'Dr. Pelletier'). Count distinct individuals; assign the category that matches the total."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ID_004",
              "name": "Types of non-human or collective agents",
              "question": "Which kinds of non-human or collective entities are treated as agents (given actions, motives, or mental states)?",
              "type": "multi_select",
              "values": [
                "none",
                "anthropomorphized animals",
                "sentient supernatural entities (spirits, gods, curses, relics)",
                "AI or digital systems",
                "institutions/personified organizations (e.g., 'the Consortium', 'the Church')",
                "collective human groups as a single agent (e.g., 'the villagers', 'the Bigwigs')"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Identify any non-individual-human entities that the narration attributes decisions, desires, feelings, or speech to. Select all categories that apply; if absolutely none, select 'none' only."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ID_005",
              "name": "Naming practice for the central character",
              "question": "How is the central character primarily identified in the narration?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "named personal name (e.g., 'Maria', 'Leon')",
                "unnamed but specific 'I/he/she' narrator",
                "role/descriptor used as main identifier (e.g., 'the mother', 'the Anchor')",
                "multiple or shifting identifiers (aliases, titles, different names in different contexts)"
              ],
              "detection_method": "For the story's most central figure, note how they are usually referred to. Choose the single label that best describes the dominant practice over the whole text."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ID_007",
              "name": "Opacity of central character at introduction",
              "question": "How transparent or mysterious is the central character's identity and role at the moment they are first introduced?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "transparent (name, role, and situation given immediately)",
                "partially opaque (some key aspects withheld or unclear)",
                "highly opaque/mysterious (identity or role deliberately obscured for an extended time)"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Examine the first scene where the central character appears. If the narration promptly states who they are and their situation, choose 'transparent'. If the reader must infer or wait for clarification of major aspects (e.g., what they are, what they want), choose a more opaque level."
            }
          ]
        },
        "inventory": {
          "aspect_name": "Character Inventory and Scale",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ID_002",
              "name": "Secondary character density",
              "question": "How many distinct secondary/supporting characters (beyond the major cast) appear in the story?",
              "type": "ordinal",
              "values": [
                "none or almost none (0\u20131)",
                "few (2\u20133)",
                "moderate (4\u20137)",
                "many (8 or more)"
              ],
              "detection_method": "List all characters who appear briefly, serve limited functions, or lack sustained interiority; exclude the major-character list from AGENT_ID_001; count and map into the ordinal bins."
            }
          ]
        },
        "naming": {
          "aspect_name": "Naming and Reference",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ID_003",
              "name": "Proportion of named vs. unnamed characters",
              "question": "Overall, how are characters referred to: mostly by proper names, by role/descriptors, or a mix?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "almost all recurring characters are given proper names",
                "mix of proper names and role-descriptors across both major and minor characters",
                "only major characters have proper names; most minor figures are role-descriptors",
                "few or no characters are named; most are referred to by roles or relational terms"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Scan the story for how recurring agents are introduced and subsequently referenced; estimate the dominant pattern across major and minor characters."
            }
          ]
        },
        "roles_and_agency": {
          "aspect_name": "Roles and Plot Agency",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ROLE_001",
              "name": "Primary functional role of the central character",
              "question": "Functionally, what role does the central character play in the story's action?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "active protagonist driving the main plot",
                "observer/witness whose main role is to watch and report on others",
                "antihero or antagonist whose actions are focalized",
                "no single central figure (true ensemble of roughly equal agents)"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Determine who the narrative follows most closely and whose choices shape key events. If that person mostly drives events, mark 'active protagonist'; if they mostly watch someone else or serve to frame another's story, choose 'observer/witness', etc."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ROLE_002",
              "name": "Nature of principal antagonistic force",
              "question": "What kinds of forces serve as the main opposition or obstacle to the central character(s)?",
              "type": "multi_select",
              "values": [
                "individual human antagonist(s)",
                "group of humans (mob, family, team)",
                "institution or system (church, corporation, legal regime)",
                "supernatural or cosmic entity",
                "environment or nature (weather, landscape, disease not personified)",
                "internal psyche/mental state of the character"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Identify what most consistently blocks or endangers the central character's goals. Select all that play a major antagonistic role (not just incidental difficulties)."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ROLE_003",
              "name": "Plot agency level of the central character",
              "question": "To what extent does the central character initiate and control key events, rather than mainly reacting to them?",
              "type": "ordinal",
              "values": [
                "mostly passive",
                "mixed",
                "mostly active"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Scan major plot turns and ask who initiates them. If the protagonist rarely chooses significant actions and is primarily acted upon, mark 'mostly passive'; if they drive most major moves, mark 'mostly active'; otherwise 'mixed'."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ROLE_004",
              "name": "Use of collective human groups as agents",
              "question": "Does the narrative treat any collective human group (e.g., 'the villagers', 'the Bigwigs', 'the kids') as a single agent with group-level intentions or feelings?",
              "type": "binary",
              "values": [
                "yes",
                "no"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Check whether any plural human groups are collectively attributed motives, decisions, or emotions (e.g., 'the villagers decided', 'the Bigwigs feared'). If so, mark 'yes'."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ROLE_005",
              "name": "Emphasis on social network versus solitude",
              "question": "How much of the story's attention is on the central character's interactions within a broader social network versus their solitary experience?",
              "type": "ordinal",
              "values": [
                "low (mostly solitary)",
                "medium",
                "high (ensemble-heavy)"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Estimate how many scenes prominently feature other named characters interacting with the central figure and how central those relationships are. If most scenes are solitary or purely introspective, choose 'low'; if many ensemble scenes drive the story, choose 'high'."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ROLE_006",
              "name": "Functions of secondary characters",
              "question": "What main functions do secondary characters serve relative to the central character?",
              "type": "multi_select",
              "values": [
                "flat types or foils (e.g., bullies, bureaucrats, stock relatives)",
                "comic relief",
                "mirrors or contrasts that highlight aspects of the central character",
                "independent subplots or mini-arcs of their own",
                "collective chorus or embodiment of 'society' or public opinion"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Review secondary characters and classify their narrative roles. Select all categories that apply to at least one reasonably prominent secondary figure."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ROLE_008",
              "name": "Presence of a frame narrator distinct from main actors",
              "question": "Is there a frame narrator whose primary role is to introduce, recount, or comment on another character's story, and who is distinct from the central acted-out protagonist?",
              "type": "binary",
              "values": [
                "yes",
                "no"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Look for an outer narrative layer (e.g., an older self, a journalist, a convent listener) that presents another character's story as a tale-within-a-tale. If such a figure exists and is not the central actor of the embedded events, mark 'yes'."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ROLE_009",
              "name": "Primary epistemic agent (who interprets the story's mysteries)",
              "question": "Who primarily discovers, interprets, or explains key information, puzzles, or moral meanings within the narrative?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "central character themselves",
                "companion or sidekick figure",
                "expert or institutional figure (detective, priest, scientist, court)",
                "external narrator/authorial commentary",
                "no clear investigative agent (mysteries left largely uninterpreted)"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Identify who asks and answers the central 'what is really happening/what does this mean' questions: the protagonist, a helper, an official expert, or an omniscient narrator. If the story leaves matters opaque with no one offering coherent interpretations, select the last option."
            }
          ]
        },
        "attributes_and_interiority": {
          "aspect_name": "Attributes, Introduction, and Interiority",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ATTR_001",
              "name": "Dominant mode of introducing the central character",
              "question": "In the first substantial appearance of the central character, what narrative device is primarily used to introduce them?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "external description (appearance/background summary)",
                "in-action event (we see them doing something significant)",
                "in-dialogue (they speak before being described)",
                "inner thought/monologue",
                "through others' reports or gossip"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Locate the passage where the central figure first shows up. Decide which element most defines that introduction: descriptive paragraphs, action, their speech, internal monologue, or someone else talking about them."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ATTR_002",
              "name": "Richness of physical description for the central character",
              "question": "How detailed is the physical description of the central character across the narrative?",
              "type": "ordinal",
              "values": [
                "none/negligible",
                "sparse (1-2 brief details)",
                "rich/elaborate"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Scan for information about the central character's body, face, clothing, or manner. If there are no more than isolated generic descriptors, mark 'none/negligible'; if there are just one or two concrete tags, 'sparse'; if multiple specific, sometimes metaphorical details appear, mark 'rich/elaborate'."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ATTR_003",
              "name": "Social identity anchors for the central character",
              "question": "Which kinds of social identity markers are used to situate the central character?",
              "type": "multi_select",
              "values": [
                "family roles (e.g., mother, son, aunt)",
                "occupation or specific skill (e.g., detective, physicist, wrestler)",
                "class, wealth, ethnicity, or nationality markers",
                "psychological label or diagnosis (e.g., autistic, depressive, 'sensitive')",
                "mythic or archetypal title (e.g., 'Anchor', 'paladin', 'final girl')",
                "legal or institutional status (e.g., suspect, prisoner, veteran)"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Note how the narration and dialogue position the character socially. Select each category explicitly invoked or strongly implied as a stable identity anchor."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ATTR_004",
              "name": "Explicit trait labeling",
              "question": "Does the narration explicitly ascribe stable personality traits to the central character (e.g., 'she was shy and stubborn') rather than only showing them through behaviour?",
              "type": "binary",
              "values": [
                "yes",
                "no"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Look for sentences that directly attribute adjectives or character traits to the protagonist as enduring qualities. If at least one such generalizing statement appears, mark 'yes'."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ATTR_005",
              "name": "Primary technique for rendering inner life",
              "question": "What is the primary narrative technique for representing the central character's inner thoughts and feelings?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "no direct access (behaviour and dialogue only)",
                "summary thought-report in narrator's voice",
                "free indirect discourse (3rd person blending narrator and character voice)",
                "quoted interior monologue or stream-of-consciousness",
                "first-person direct reporting of thoughts ('I thought...')"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Examine passages where the character's mental states appear. Identify whether these are reported indirectly in a narrator's idiom, slip into the character's diction while in 3rd person, appear as direct quotes of thought, or are framed as 'I' reflections; choose the technique that dominates."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ATTR_006",
              "name": "Psychological depth scale for central character",
              "question": "On a 1\u20135 scale, how psychologically complex is the central character (considering contradictions, backstory, evolving self-understanding)?",
              "type": "scale",
              "values": [
                "1",
                "2",
                "3",
                "4",
                "5"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Judge holistically: 1 = very flat (few inner details, mostly role-function), 3 = some inner conflict and backstory but relatively simple, 5 = highly detailed, self-contradictory, and evolving psychological portrait. Assign intermediate scores (2 or 4) as needed."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ATTR_009",
              "name": "Closure of central character's psychological arc",
              "question": "By the end, does the narrative present the central character's internal trajectory as having reached a clear resting point (even if tragic), rather than halting mid-crisis?",
              "type": "binary",
              "values": [
                "yes",
                "no"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Assess whether the story resolves the protagonist's main inner conflict, offering a stable new state or accepted impasse, versus cutting off at a moment of acute unresolved tension. If the latter, mark 'no'."
            }
          ]
        },
        "introduction": {
          "aspect_name": "Introduction and Backstory Placement",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "AGENT_ATTR_008",
              "name": "Staggered vs. batch introduction of core cast",
              "question": "Are core characters introduced gradually over time or in an early exposition cluster?",
              "type": "binary",
              "values": [
                "staggered introduction across the story",
                "batch introduction early in the story"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Note when each major character (AGENT_ID_001 list) first appears; if most majors arrive in the first one or two scenes/chapters, choose 'batch'; if they enter at clearly different later points, choose 'staggered'."
            }
          ]
        },
        "emotion": {
          "aspect_name": "Emotional Expression",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "AGENT_EMO_009",
              "name": "Dominant mode of emotional expression",
              "question": "How are characters' emotions most commonly conveyed?",
              "type": "categorical",
              "values": [
                "explicit_emotion_labels",
                "embodied_sensations_and_metaphors",
                "behavioral_cues_and_action_only",
                "consistently_ambiguous_or_suppressed"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Review scenes with strong affect. If emotions are usually named directly (e.g., 'she was angry, terrified'), choose 'explicit_emotion_labels'. If emotions are more often shown via bodily states or metaphors (tight throat, weights on chest, storm imagery), choose 'embodied_sensations_and_metaphors'. If feelings are mostly inferred from what characters do and say without explicit naming or sensory description, choose 'behavioral_cues_and_action_only'. If the narration avoids or undercuts emotional disclosure so that states remain unclear, choose 'consistently_ambiguous_or_suppressed'."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_EMO_012",
              "name": "Preferred cues for conveying emotional state",
              "question": "Which textual cues are most commonly used to convey what characters are feeling?",
              "type": "multi_select",
              "values": [
                "bodily sensations or physiology (e.g., heartbeat, nausea, tight chest)",
                "facial expressions or gestures (e.g., frowns, smiles, posture)",
                "action choices and behavior (e.g., slamming doors, withdrawing, calling someone)",
                "metaphorical or environmental mirroring (weather, setting, or images echoing mood)",
                "dialogue content and tone (what and how characters speak)"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Review emotionally charged scenes and note which kinds of cues recur most often when feelings are being conveyed; select all categories that are prominent rather than incidental."
            }
          ]
        },
        "motivation": {
          "aspect_name": "Motivations & Goals",
          "features": [
            {
              "id": "AGENT_MOT_003",
              "name": "Dominant sources of motivation",
              "question": "Which sources most strongly drive the central character's actions?",
              "type": "multi_select",
              "values": [
                "personal desire or ambition",
                "ethical or ideological principles",
                "social or familial obligations",
                "trauma or past hurt",
                "economic survival or material necessity",
                "supernatural or external compulsion"
              ],
              "detection_method": "For major choices, identify what is invoked as the underlying drive (explicitly or implicitly). Select each source that clearly and repeatedly shapes important actions."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_MOT_004",
              "name": "Evolution of motivations over time",
              "question": "Does the central character's primary motivation clearly change or develop over the course of the narrative?",
              "type": "binary",
              "values": [
                "yes",
                "no"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Compare early and late aims. If the story marks a shift (e.g., from self-preservation to protecting others; from revenge to forgiveness), or shows a goal fading and another emerging, mark 'yes'. If core motivations stay essentially constant, mark 'no'."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_MOT_011",
              "name": "Explicitness of character motivations",
              "question": "How explicitly are characters' motivations stated in the narration or dialogue?",
              "type": "ordinal",
              "values": [
                "mostly_implict_or_inferred",
                "occasionally_stated_internally",
                "frequently_spelled_out_in_dialogue_or_narration"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Check whether reasons for key actions are primarily left for the reader to infer, occasionally voiced in inner monologue or reflection, or often spelled out explicitly (e.g., 'He did it because he could not bear the thought of\u2026'). Classify according to the most common practice across important characters and scenes.",
              "merged_from": [
                "AGENT_MOT_001",
                "AGENT_MOT_013"
              ]
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_MOT_012",
              "name": "Typical motivation domains for major characters",
              "question": "Which motivation domains most frequently drive major characters' actions?",
              "type": "multi_select",
              "values": [
                "survival_or_physical_safety",
                "family_or_romantic_relationships",
                "ideological_or_moral_commitments",
                "curiosity_or_epistemic_drive",
                "ambition_status_or_power",
                "guilt_shame_or_desire_for_atonement"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Identify the main goals behind protagonists' and key antagonists' decisions across stories. For each, assign one or more domains (e.g., protecting loved ones, uncovering truth, seeking promotion, making amends). Select all domains that recur as primary motivators for several central characters."
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_MOT_014",
              "name": "Complexity of protagonist motivation",
              "question": "How complex are the protagonist's motives across the story?",

                "single, relatively stable goal or desire dominates",
                "multiple but largely compatible goals or desires",
                "conflicted or ambivalent motives are central (the protagonist is pulled in opposing directions)"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Identify the protagonist's stated or implied goals across the narrative; assess whether they (a) stay singular and stable, (b) branch but remain aligned, or (c) involve sustained internal conflict between incompatible aims.",
              "merged_from": [
                "AGENT_MOT_002"
              ]
            },
            {
              "id": "AGENT_MOT_016",

                "psychological self-understanding (e.g., insight into self, trauma, desires)",
                "relational role shift (e.g., from outsider to insider, dependent to caregiver)",
                "status or power change (e.g., social rank, professional role, authority)",
                "ontological or metaphysical transformation (e.g., becoming non-human, godlike, or altered in reality-status)"
              ],
              "detection_method": "Identify the main before/after difference in the protagonist (if any); choose the category that best captures the core transformation emphasized by the narrative."
            }
          ]
        },
        "archetypes_and_tropes": {
          "aspect_name": "Archetypes & Tropes",
          "features": [

              "id": "AGENT_TRP_001",
